candidate.quote:
Twice a hundred dawns, a hundred noons, a hundred eves._

[p00242] \u201cYou see there were two dawns to every noon and evening--it must have

candidate.paraphrase: A verse describes an almanac with two dawns for every noon and evening, an altered temporal ordering.

criteria.rationale: The text is a political satire in the Alice/Looking-Glass idiom. References to 'Natural History,' 'science of knowing when things are over,' or Christian Science are jokes, not any material representation of scientific fact, theory, discovery, or natural process. No genuine scientific content drives the work.

The White Knight boasts of his 'own invention'--a short-range gun designed to be useless to the enemy. This is a satirical invention rather than an engineered system that materially shapes a speculative setting; it is a lampoon of policy, so interpretation and materiality are uncertain.

The Unkhaki Messenger is described as perpetually 'half a century in front of his times or half a century behind,' a figurative temporal displacement used satirically. It gestures at time-dislocation but is metaphor rather than an actual speculative future or literal time travel.

The White Queen extrapolates a Christian-Science premise to its absurd political consequence--that convincing her reasoning faculty the war does not exist would end it--and Alice pushes the consequence further. This is developed satirical extrapolation from a social/ideological premise, though its speculative status is uncertain.

Characters ask questions and 'unravel the groundwork of what people believe,' but this is portrayed as ineffectual muddle, not observation, hypothesis, testing, measurement, or systematic inference materially driving understanding. No genuine scientific method operates.

The entire setting is a Looking-Glass/Wonderland otherworld--a nonordinary dimension inhabited by pasteboard playing-card beings--and the storyworld's existence is contingent on the Red King's dream. This is a substantially nonordinary environment, though as literary allegory rather than a cosmic/planetary novum, so interpretation is uncertain.

The South African war is referenced as satirical backdrop, and the dream-collapse ('go piff') is a whimsical conceit rather than a depicted large-scale disaster that is actual, impending, or causally central to the narrative. No catastrophe materially drives the story.

candidates.description: The entire storyworld is a Looking-Glass/Wonderland political allegory in which Edwardian British politicians and institutions are transformed into Carrollian chesspiece and playing-card creatures made of pasteboard and Brummagem ware, governed by an inverted 'topsy-turvy' logic where inaction, non-decision, and make-believe are the operative rules.

novelty.rationale: The introductory verse and narrative frame a totalizing inversion of the empirical world ('Turvey-wise', 'Backwards through a Looking-Glass'), and the figures are literally reconstituted as pasteboard/Brummagem-ware card beings and dream-contingent creatures, altering the ontological basis of the whole story universe.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The world follows a consistent internal allegorical/satirical logic (the 'Rules of the Game', characters as card-pack constructs, the Red King's dream premise) but this logic is drawn directly from Carroll's fantasy nonsense conceits rather than a systematic, immanent, nonsupernatural cognitive account; the dream-contingent existence in particular leans toward the fantastic rather than an estranging science or social organization.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The Looking-Glass allegorical frame governs every episode and determines the overriding narrative logic; it is not an incidental device but the organizing principle of the whole text.

estrangement.rationale: The reader encounters familiar political realities defamiliarized as a nonsense looking-glass world, with the introductory verse explicitly signalling the inversion and the tea-table's seven-year-old menu contrasting promise with inaction.

candidates.description: A social/mental principle in which reality is governed by belief and reasoning rather than material fact: the White Queen proposes ending a war simply by convincing her reasoning faculty it does not exist, and creatures fear they will cease to exist when the Red King wakes from his dream.

novelty.rationale: The idea that belief governs material reality would be a world-altering difference from the empirical norm, but here it is presented as satirical mockery of 'Christian Science' and political evasion rather than an established operative law of the storyworld; Alice's objection undercuts its actual efficacy.

cognitive_validation.rationale: No coherent, systematic, immanent account of belief-governed reality is developed; it is offered as ridicule and immediately shown not to work, lacking the internal consistency a novum's cognitive logic requires.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The belief-as-reality motif is a localized satirical exchange in one episode and does not determine the overriding logic of the whole narrative.

estrangement.rationale: The reader is estranged by political inaction literalized as the doctrine that wars can be wished out of existence, contrasting sharply with material reality.

candidates.description: The White Knight's self-invented military technology and doctrine of waging war 'not under modern conditions', including short-range guns deliberately useless to the enemy.

novelty.rationale: These are satirical gadgets and antiquated tactics; they do not constitute a totalizing, world-altering difference from the empirical norm but rather mock incompetent military planning within an otherwise recognizable world.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The Knight gives a pseudo-rational explanation for his gun design, but it is comic absurdity rather than a systematic imaginary science governing the world.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The Knight's inventions are an incidental episodic satirical device and do not determine the overriding narrative logic.

estrangement.rationale: The reader is estranged by the defamiliarization of military planning into deliberately self-defeating gadgetry, but this remains an incidental gadget rather than a world premise.
